Taiwan shares end slightly higher on late buying of TSMC
sum: Taipei, Nov. 27 (CNA) Taiwan shares closed slightly higher Friday after a directionless session with U.S. markets closed overnight for Thanksgiving, with late-session buying of contract chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) supporting the broader market, dealers said.

The Taiex, the Taiwan Stock Exchange's benchmark index, ended up 156.27 points, or 0.40 percent, at 39,308.08 after fluctuating between 38,890.53 and 39,495.41. Turnover totaled NT$666.07 billion (US$20.22 billion), down from NT$845.34 billion Thursday.

"Look at the reduced turnover. I think the Taiex had no cues from Wall Street today because U.S. markets were closed so that the index just drifted without any direction throughout the session," Concord Securities analyst Kerry Huang said.

"After recent wild swings, the Taiex has entered a consolidation phase as many investors stayed on the sidelines, waiting for fresh catalysts," Huang said. "Select large-cap stocks, particularly TSMC, attracted buying in the last minutes of the session, maintaining the broader market's strength."

TSMC, which accounts for over 40 percent of the Taiwanese stock market's total capitalization, rose 1.63 percent to close at NT$2,180.00. Its gains contributed about 280 points to the Taiex, offsetting losses elsewhere in the market.

Among other semiconductor stocks, smartphone integrated circuit (IC) designer MediaTek Inc. fell 0.67 percent to NT$3,680.00, and United Microelectronics Corp., a smaller contract chipmaker, closed down 1.46 percent at NT$87.50. IC packaging and testing firm ASE Technology Holding Co. rose 0.59 percent to NT$514.00.

Elsewhere in the tech sector, iPhone assembler and artificial intelligence (AI) server maker Hon Hai Precision Industry Co. rose 1.15 percent to close at NT$219.00, and power management solutions provider Delta Electronics Inc. gained 0.45 percent to close at NT$1,125.00.

items.t: Hon Hai's FoxBrain Takes Second Place Globally in Taiwan Sovereign AI Benchmark, Punching Above Its Weight at 31B Parameters
sum: FoxBrain v2.1, the latest large language model from the Hon Hai Research Institute (HHRI), a unit of Hon Hai Technology Group (2317.TW), has been ranked second globally in the "Taiwan Sovereign AI Basic Benchmark Indicators" run by the Ministry of Digital Affairs' AI Product and System Evaluation Center (AIEC), based on data compiled to date. The result gives Hon Hai international visibility in the self-developed language model field and prompts a fresh look at its technology positioning at the AI software layer.

The benchmark was launched in March 2025 as a baseline study of domestic and foreign language models, and in October of the same year the first results for 42 models were published. It focuses on three indicators — classical Chinese literacy (based on the Chinese portion of Taiwan's college entrance exam), civic literacy (based on the social studies portion) and core Taiwanese values — using question sets to observe how models perform in local linguistic contexts and value judgments.
Accuracy Rates for the Three Indicators; Taiwanese Values Beat International Models

FoxBrain v2.1 posted accuracy rates of 96.20% on classical Chinese literacy, 91.37% on civic literacy and 98.00% on core Taiwanese values. On the Taiwanese values indicator, it topped the 72.00% to 94.00% range recorded by all international models currently on the compiled list; on the Chinese and social studies portions, it beat the best results of other domestic models on the list by about 9.4 and 4.2 percentage points, respectively.

Note: Data are results published by the Hon Hai Research Institute under the AIEC's "Taiwan Sovereign AI Basic Benchmark Indicators" and reflect performance under specific question sets and test conditions.

Li Yung-hui, director of the AI research division at the Hon Hai Research Institute, said FoxBrain's development has focused on data construction, model training and alignment, and deep reasoning capabilities that meet industry needs. The benchmark data, Li said, gave the team concrete metrics to review its R&D results and to compare against international models within the same evaluation scope.

Hon Hai stock: Foxconn faces USD 15 million India dispute
sum: Foxconn faces a fresh legal dispute in India after vendor BCD Emprassa took a claim of about USD 15 million to the National Company Law Tribunal. The Economic Times reported the development on Wednesday, November 25, citing a statement from Hon Hai Technology Group, better known as Foxconn.

Foxconn said the disagreement arose from BCD Emprassa's failure to meet agreed contractual requirements and quality standards. The company said repeated requests for corrective action had not resolved the outstanding issues and that it would take appropriate steps to protect its rights in the judicial process.

The vendor's claim concerns housing and related services for Foxconn employees at its Bengaluru facility. The Economic Times reported that the dispute involves roughly 700 residential units leased for employees, while the supplier is seeking recovery through India's insolvency tribunal.

The dispute adds a legal risk to Foxconn's expanding manufacturing presence in India, a key production location for global electronics companies including Apple. Foxconn said it values long-standing supplier relationships and remains committed to conducting business in good faith.

For investors, the immediate issue is the legal process and the parties' competing accounts of contractual performance. The public statement does not resolve the claim or indicate a final financial outcome.

Hon Hai stock: Foxconn to acquire Sony automotive camera unit
sum: On November 17, 2026, Hon Hai Technology Group, widely known as Foxconn, announced that it will acquire Sony Semiconductor Solutions' automotive camera module business. The company said the transaction is intended to deepen its position in automotive electronics and smart mobility. The announcement was published by Hon Hai Technology Group.

The acquisition is being carried out through Rayprus Japan, a wholly owned Foxconn subsidiary. It is intended to include the business's operations, technologies, customer relationships and operating resources.

Foxconn said it plans to use the acquired technology, customer base and direct-to-automaker experience to strengthen its integrated automotive service capabilities. The move adds an automotive imaging operation to a group that has long developed, manufactured and integrated camera modules for information and communications technology applications.

The initial transaction amount is estimated at 7.24 billion Japanese yen. That figure excludes other assets still under discussion, including relevant overseas production equipment and inventory, and Foxconn said the final purchase amount may be adjusted under the transaction framework.

Sony Semiconductor Solutions is a key supplier of automotive camera modules with established relationships with global automakers, according to Foxconn. The buyer said the parties will initially focus on customer continuity and operational stability. Relevant overseas entities are expected to continue operating and provide transitional support after closing.

Foxconn expects the transaction to close by the end of April 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions. For investors, the strategic rationale is clear, while the financial contribution cannot yet be assessed from the announced terms because the release does not provide the acquired business's revenue or profit.

Taiwan Stock Market Falls 6.2% to Cap Its Worst Week Since 1991 as KOSPI Closes Down 5.2% and Nikkei 225 Drops 5.1% in AI Chip Selloff
sum: This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Taiwan’s stock market fell 6.2% on Friday to cap its worst week since 1991. South Korea’s KOSPI closed down 5.2% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 5.1%. All three lost more than 5% as the selloff in AI chip stocks that began on Wall Street ran through a full Asian session. On Thursday the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.3% and the S&P 500 2.0% after Advanced Micro Devices sank 7.7% on a short seller’s report.

For the week, Taiwan’s Taiex lost 17.5%, the KOSPI 7.9% and the Nikkei 7.7%. Bloomberg called it Taiwan’s worst week since 1991. Reuters reported during the session that MSCI’s index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was down 8.3% for the week, its worst since March 2020.

The closes read as a sign that sellers stayed in control to the end: Seoul and Tokyo finished lower than they stood at midday, and the Nikkei closed at its low of the day. That reading has a limit. Tokyo is shut Monday for a holiday, which gave traders a reason to sell before the weekend, and U.S. futures point to a smaller loss on Wall Street than Thursday’s.
The Taiex closed at 36,033.29, down 2,394 points. It has lost 7,642 points since last Friday.

The KOSPI closed at 4,869.96, down 268 points, its lowest close since Jan. 16. It was down 4.6% at midday. The exchange paused program selling for five minutes on the KOSPI before noon and on the Kosdaq in the afternoon.
The Nikkei 225 closed at 56,436.65, down 3,008 points. That is a seven-month low and 23% below its 52-week high. The index was down 4.5% at the lunch break. The broader Topix lost 3.9%.

items.t: US Stock Selloff Drags Taiwan Stocks Down 1,395 Points at Open; TSMC Falls NT$60, Delta Electronics Slips Below NT$1,000

items.t: Taiwan Stocks Plunge 1,768 Points, Break Below Annual Line; Market Value Wipes Out Over NT$5 Trillion in a Single Day as Foreign Investors Sell Only NT$24.3 Billion
sum: Taiwan stocks came under rare and heavy selling pressure on the 19th. The weighted index fell steadily after the open, successively losing the 40,000 and 39,000 integer levels intraday, touching a low of 38,259.70 — a drop of 1,935.21 points — before closing at 38,426.89, down 4.40%. That marked the seventh-largest closing decline in the history of the Taiwan stock market, with turnover of NT$895.281 billion (approximately $27.2 billion). The index also broke below its annual line at around 39,368, signaling the loss of a key long-term bull-bear dividing line.

In terms of market value, the total capitalization of listed companies shrank to about NT$125.9 trillion (approximately $3.8 trillion) in a single day, evaporating more than NT$5 trillion (approximately $151.8 billion) from the previous day and falling below the NT$131 trillion (approximately $4.0 trillion) mark. The decline spread from large-cap electronics stocks to small and mid-caps and traditional industries, with the number of limit-down stocks at one point approaching 300 — a breadth of selling rarely seen recently.

Weighted stocks were the main source of the selloff. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (2330.TW) closed down NT$75, or 3.45%, at NT$2,100, single-handedly dragging the index down 577.97 points — about one-third of the total decline. MediaTek (2454.TW) plunged NT$220, or 5.58%, to NT$3,720, contributing 102.60 points to the decline. ASE Technology Holding (3711.TW) tumbled NT$44, or 8.03%, to NT$504. Delta Electronics (2308.TW) fell NT$60, or 5.66%, narrowly holding the NT$1,000 level. Hon Hai (2317.TW) was relatively resilient, slipping just NT$0.5, or 0.23%, to close at NT$220.5.

Other electronics sectors could not escape the adjustment either, with substrate, thermal and memory stocks under heavy selling. Unimicron Technology (3037.TW) closed limit-down at NT$596; Asia Vital Components (3017.TW) closed limit-down at NT$2,445; Global Unichip (3443.TW) closed limit-down at NT$6,000; and Jentech Precision Industrial (3653.TW) closed limit-down at NT$4,115. In memory, Nanya Technology (2408.TW) plunged NT$31.5, or 9.69%, to NT$293.5. Among passive components, Walsin Technology (2492.TW) and Holy Stone Enterprise (3026.TW) both closed limit-down, while Yageo (2327.TW) fell 8.38%.

sum: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced his resignation from the CEO and board positions amid an extramarital affair scandal. After the negative news settled over the weekend, it detonated fully on Monday (the 16th), with Taiwan stocks opening lower and selling pressure continuously expanding. Intraday, the TAIEX at one point plunged more than 2,000 points, successively breaking through the two round-number thresholds of 43,000 and 42,000. None of the five major weighted stocks was spared, and power management giant Delta Electronics (2308.TW) was directly slammed to its limit-down price of NT$1,120.

The TAIEX opened at 43,512.42 on the 16th, down 162.70 points, before the decline quickly spiraled out of control. Intraday it fell to a low of 41,591.36, a plunge of 2,083.76 points. If the decline does not narrow by the close, it will mark a rare record for single-day point losses in Taiwan stock market history.

The selling was concentrated in large-cap electronics stocks. Foundry leader Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (2330.TW) closed at NT$2,350 last Friday. On the 16th it opened slightly lower at NT$2,340 and weakened steadily, touching an intraday low of NT$2,260, down NT$90, or 3.83%, on volume of 23,000 lots. Market observers attribute the decline to several factors, including the slower-than-expected development of 5G open radio access networks (O-RAN), the failure of its low-earth-orbit (LEO) satellite business to contribute profits in time, and the severe blow dealt to its subsidiaries by the U.S.-China trade war.

sum: Taiwan's Weighted Index opened lower and fell further on the 3rd, touching an intraday low of 43,191.58 before closing down 1,612.60 points, or 3.59%, at 43,307.54 — decisively breaking below the 44,000-point threshold — with single-day turnover of NT$928.058 billion (approximately $28.3 billion). Measured over the past month, the benchmark has now tumbled roughly 6,000 points, and concerns over whether a bear market has officially arrived are heating up rapidly. Moore Investment Advisory Chief Investment Officer Guo Zherong stepped forward at this juncture, citing the latest Nomura Securities report to argue that the selloff stems from excessive market sentiment rather than a deterioration in corporate fundamentals. He stressed that "the market will eventually give fundamentals their due."

Guo Zherong analyzed that the market has been continuously magnifying political uncertainty ahead of the U.S. election as well as the disruption to oil prices and market sentiment from shifting U.S.-Iran tensions. These headline factors have become reasons for investors to sell holdings, but they should not be equated directly with a deteriorating corporate profit outlook. He believes that once panic gradually subsides, capital will ultimately re-examine corporate earnings and industry trends, giving the market a chance to return to fundamentals. He therefore maintained his medium- to long-term view that the Taiwan Weighted Index will challenge 50,000 by year-end and reach 100,000 over the next three years.

The Nomura Securities report cited by Guo Zherong centers on clarifying a misunderstanding about the AI industry. The report notes that investors have directly interpreted cloud giants' "negative free cash flow" as "AI is unprofitable and earnings are declining," when in fact they are conflating two concepts: profit and cash flow. Cloud providers are currently in the early stage of heavy investment in AI infrastructure, aggressively purchasing GPUs and developing their own TPU chips; it is the massive capital expenditure that has temporarily turned cash flow negative. Yet the three major cloud providers posted year-on-year revenue growth of 56% over the same period, showing that real demand for AI computing power remains strong.

items.t: 2026: AI Servers to Be Extremely Expensive
sum: In 2026, it will be a crucial window period for the system-level upgrade of AI servers.

Correspondingly, there will be more effective power supply solutions, standard liquid cooling solutions, and higher requirements for PCBs and high-speed interconnections. This system-level upgrade will also make AI servers in 2026 "incredibly expensive."

Morgan Stanley predicts that for NVIDIA's platform alone, the demand for AI server cabinets will soar from approximately 28,000 units in 2025 to at least 60,000 units in 2026, more than doubling. Meanwhile, AMD's Helios server rack project (based on the MI400 series) has also made good progress, further intensifying the market's demand for advanced AI hardware.
Currently, NVIDIA's Blackwell platform, especially the GB200 chip, is the core driving force in the current AI server market.
In 2026, AI hardware will shift from the H00/H200 era to a new cycle driven by NVIDIA's GB200/300 (Blackwell platform) and the subsequent Vera Rubin (VR series) platform.

The power consumption of chips continues to break through the upper limit. From the 700W TDP (TDP: Thermal Design Power) of the H100, to 1000W of the B200, then to 1200W of the GB200, and finally to the Vera Rubin (VR200) platform that will debut in the second half of 2026, the maximum TDP of its GPU will soar to 2300W, and the VR200 NVL44 CPX at the end of 2026 will reach as high as 3700W.

As the GPU power consumption approaches 4kW, traditional air cooling solutions are completely ineffective, and liquid cooling has become the only viable option. NVIDIA has made liquid cooling a standard configuration on the GB200 platform and is jointly developing customized cold plate interfaces with major OEM manufacturers to ensure efficient heat transfer to the cooling circuit.

"There's been a lot of talk about an AI bubble," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told investors on an earnings call, as the firm set out its view of the industry. "From our vantage point, we see something very different."

The blowout quarter exceeded even the whisper numbers for the AI chip leader, and while most major analysts commented on and touted the positives, Ross Seymore at Deutsche Bank noted that the shares are "fairly valued."

Nvidia's upbeat guidance helped lift investor sentiment around the AI trade, which has weakened in recent sessions amid fears about elevated valuations, debt financing and potential chip depreciation.

The results boosted a slew of stocks across the AI ecosystem immecdiately following the report, including chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom and power infrastructure companies such as Eaton.
Shares of each company sank Thursday as part of the broader market turnaround.

AI data center mostly booked: Hon Hai
sum: Manufacturing giant Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密) yesterday said that clients have already booked 70 to 80 percent of the computing power at its artificial intelligence (AI) data center in Kaohsiung.
Hon Hai in May announced a partnership with Nvidia Corp to build the data center in the city’s Asia New Bay Area (亞洲新灣區).

Hon Hai said it would purchase 10,000 GB300 chips based on Nvidia’s Blackwell Ultra architecture to provide up to 27MW of computing power in the center’s first phase of development, positioning it as a local AI inference hub.
Four clients have booked computing power at the data center, Hon Hai spokesman James Wu (巫俊毅) said on the sidelines of a news conference in Taipei, without naming the clients.
The center is to begin operations in the first half of next year, with a second phase of development being planned, Hon Hai said.

The company has intensified its efforts in AI development in the past few years to diversify its product portfolio. Last month, the company’s board of directors approved a NT$42 billion (US$1.345 billion) investment plan to purchase AI equipment for the data center.
Hon Hai plans to grow its AI deployment vertically and horizontally, Wu said.

items.t: Hon Hai reports record-high Q3 profit
sum: Manufacturing giant Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密) yesterday posted its best third-quarter profit in the company’s history, backed by strong demand for artificial intelligence (AI) servers.
Net profit expanded 17 percent annually to NT$57.67 billion (US$1.86 billion) from NT$44.36 billion, the company said.
On a quarterly basis, net profit soared 30 percent from NT$44.36 billion, it said.

Hon Hai, which is Apple Inc’s primary iPhone assembler and makes servers powered by Nvidia Corp’s AI accelerators, said earnings per share expanded to NT$4.15 from NT$3.55 a year earlier and NT$3.19 in the second quarter.

Gross margin improved to 6.35 percent, up from 6.19 percent a year earlier and 6.33 percent in the previous quarter, which the company attributed to better vertical integration of its products and a larger operational scale.

The growth momentum in AI servers is expected to extend into next year and the following two to three years, as the “major five” cloud service providers have raised their capital expenditure to about US$600 billion for next year, Hon Hai chairman Young Liu (劉揚偉) told investors yesterday.

“I am very optimistic about the development of the AI market next year. Our cooperation with clients and partners will be closer, and we expect to secure more orders by engaging in a wider range of AI projects,” Liu said. “Briefly, I am very positive about our outlook for 2026.”
